displayQuote: Nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power

meta.title: Who really said "Nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Lincoln never said it. The line traces to orator Robert G. Ingersoll, who in an 1883 lecture praised Lincoln’s use of power — and was later misquoted as Lincoln.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power'?
meta.ogDescription: Lincoln never said it. It traces to orator Robert G. Ingersoll’s 1883 lecture praising Lincoln — later flipped into words put in Lincoln’s mouth.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — actually Robert G. Ingersoll
answer.sourceLine: Lincoln never said or wrote this. The idea comes from orator Robert G. Ingersoll, who in an 1883 lecture on Lincoln declared, “Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is give him power. This is the supreme test” — words about Lincoln that were later flattened into a quote by him. See Quote Investigator ↗.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Nothing discloses real character like the use of power. It is easy for the weak to be gentle. Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is give him power. This is the supreme test.
trail: Precursor: Thomas Carlyle wrote in 1841 that “for one man who can stand prosperity, there are a hundred that will stand adversity,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
Ingersoll’s 1883 lecture gave the modern formulation: “if you wish to know what a man really is give him power. This is the supreme test,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
The exact condensed wording “Nearly all men can stand adversity…” was first printed with Lincoln’s name in 1931 (Williamsburg Journal-Tribune, Iowa), per Quote Investigator ↗.
Snopes ↗ and Check Your Fact ↗ both rate the Lincoln attribution False.
source.cutTag: ↑ Ingersoll’s original — the polished “Nearly all men can stand adversity” version came decades later
source.excerptNote: Ingersoll spoke these words in praise of Lincoln’s restraint, continuing that it was “the glory of Lincoln that, having almost absolute power, he never abused it, except on the side of mercy.” The subject of the tribute later got mistaken for its author.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: full chronology of the quote

source.rightsNote: Ingersoll’s original text (1883–1895) is in the public domain. The polished “Nearly all men can stand adversity” wording is a later paraphrase of unknown authorship and is not a genuine Lincoln quotation.

author.name: Robert G. Ingersoll
author.heading: Robert G. Ingersoll
author.bio: Robert Green Ingersoll (1833–1899) was a Civil War veteran, Illinois attorney general, and the most celebrated American orator of the Gilded Age, nicknamed “The Great Agnostic.” A great admirer of Lincoln, he delivered a widely reprinted lecture on him in the early 1880s. His tribute to Lincoln’s merciful use of power — not any words of Lincoln’s own — is the origin of this quotation.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: Almost universally credited to Abraham Lincoln on posters, mugs, and leadership slides — but the words are neither his nor even from his lifetime.

items.why: Lincoln died in 1865; the sentiment first appears in Robert Ingersoll’s lecture praising Lincoln, published in 1883, and the exact modern wording was not tied to Lincoln’s name until about 1931. Per Snopes ↗, Lincoln “never uttered or wrote those words, or words to that effect.”

Ingersoll actually said, “Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is give him power. This is the supreme test,” per Quote Investigator ↗. The tidy “Nearly all men can stand adversity” version is a later paraphrase.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the words were spoken about Lincoln by Robert G. Ingersoll — then, over decades of retelling, put into Lincoln’s mouth. See Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ingersoll’s point was a tribute, not a maxim: he argued that power, not hardship, is the real test of character, and that Lincoln passed it by wielding near-absolute wartime authority with mercy. The irony is that a line composed to honor Lincoln’s restraint was eventually rewritten as if Lincoln were dispensing the wisdom himself.
Because the polished version scans like a stump-speech aphorism — and because Lincoln is a magnet for orphaned quotations — the misattribution spread far faster than the correction.
context.pull: Words said about Lincoln became words said by Lincoln.
